title: Research
text: Many processes follow a known kind of dynamic, such as exponential growth, a burning rate or the course of an epidemic, but real data about them are often sparse, irregular or clustered. Standard curve-fitting methods lose accuracy exactly where the data are thinnest, while fully parametric differential-equation models break down when the assumed equation is only approximately right.

title: Research
text: Many processes follow a known kind of dynamic, such as exponential growth, a burning rate or the course of an epidemic, but real data about them are often sparse, irregular or clustered. Standard curve-fitting methods lose accuracy exactly where the data are thinnest, while fully parametric differential-equation models break down when the assumed equation is only approximately right.

title: Research
text:
My approach
My PhD thesis, Differential Equation-Constrained Local Polynomial Regression Models (UBC Okanagan, 2026; supervisor Dr. W. John Braun), develops a unified framework, DE-LPR, that builds differential-equation information directly into local polynomial regression. The estimator borrows structure from the equation where data are scarce and stays flexible where they are plentiful.
The framework covers five model classes:

Exponential growth: first-order ODE constraints, with theory for bias, variance and bandwidth selection
Quasi-exponential growth: growth rates that drift over time
General linear ODEs
General nonlinear ODEs, benchmarked against parameter-cascade (PCODE) methods
Second- and higher-order ODEs

Across these, the DE-constrained estimators achieve lower asymptotic bias than conventional local polynomial estimators of the same degree while keeping comparable variance, and they perform markedly better under sparse designs.

title: Research
text:

🔥 Fire science

title: HIV Clinical Trial Survival Analysis (SAS)
text:
A complete survival analysis of AIDS Clinical Trials Group Study 175, a randomized trial of 2,139 adults with HIV comparing four antiretroviral regimens. The full workflow, from data preparation to Cox models, subgroup analyses and restricted mean survival time, was built in SAS, and the key models were reproduced in R.
View the code on GitHub ↗
Highlights

title: HIV Clinical Trial Survival Analysis (SAS)
text:
Data
ACTG 175 (Hammer et al., NEJM 1996), obtained from the UCI Machine Learning Repository. Patients were randomized to ZDV only, ZDV + didanosine (ddI), ZDV + zalcitabine (Zal), or ddI only. The primary endpoint is a composite of a ≥50% decline in CD4 count, progression to AIDS, or death.

Adjusted for age, weight, Karnofsky score, baseline CD4 and CD8, sex, race, haemophilia, homosexual activity, injection drug use, symptoms and prior antiretroviral therapy.
Proportional hazards. Baseline CD4 clearly violated proportional hazards, so a sensitivity model stratified by baseline CD4 quartile was fitted; treatment effects were essentially unchanged (HRs 0.45, 0.50, 0.56). For treatment, the SAS supremum test supported proportional hazards (p ≥ 0.11), while the Schoenfeld residual test in R suggested mild non-proportionality (p = 0.03). The hazard ratios are therefore read as time-averaged effects, and RMST is reported alongside them.

CD4 response. In an ANCOVA adjusted for baseline CD4, mean CD4 count fell by 16 cells/mm³ at week 20 on ZDV only and rose on all other regimens. Adjusted differences versus ZDV only were +70 (ZDV + ddI), +36 (ZDV + Zal) and +42 (ddI only) cells/mm³ (Dunnett-adjusted p < 0.0001). The benefit was larger among patients with lower baseline CD4 (arm-by-baseline interaction p = 0.0015). Notably, ZDV + ddI produced the largest CD4 gain even though the three newer regimens did not differ in the clinical endpoint, a reminder that a surrogate marker and a clinical outcome can tell different stories.

title: HIV Clinical Trial Survival Analysis (SAS)
HIV Clinical Trial Survival Analysis (SAS)
text:
Validation in R
Hazard ratios from all Cox models, the log-rank statistic (χ² = 49.19), the ANCOVA estimates and the RMST values matched between SAS and R to at least five decimal places. One detail worth knowing: SAS PROC PHREG defaults to Breslow ties while R coxph() defaults to Efron, so the two packages disagree slightly unless the method is set explicitly. In this dataset the two methods give nearly identical results because each tied event time involves only one to three events against risk sets of several hundred patients.

title: HIV Clinical Trial Survival Analysis (SAS)
text:
Limitations and next steps
ACTG 175 is a randomized controlled trial, not observational registry data, so the estimated treatment effects are not affected by confounding by indication. Subgroup analyses are exploratory and were not powered for subgroup-specific conclusions. A natural next step is to simulate an observational cohort from these data and apply propensity score methods, the setting typical of HIV registry research.
Data: Hammer SM et al. (1996). A trial comparing nucleoside monotherapy with combination therapy in HIV-infected adults with CD4 cell counts from 200 to 500 per cubic millimeter. New England Journal of Medicine, 335(15), 1081–1090. Dataset accessed via the UCI Machine Learning Repository (ID 890).

title: Curve Estimation from Sparse Data
text:
My PhD work developed statistical methods that combine differential equations with local polynomial regression, so that curves can be estimated accurately even where data are sparse.
Highlights

Built a unified estimation framework covering exponential, quasi-exponential, linear, nonlinear and higher-order ODE models
Proved lower asymptotic bias than standard local polynomial estimators at comparable variance
Ran extensive simulation studies under uniform and sparse designs
Applied the methods to firebrand burning-rate data, Korean influenza surveillance data and tumour growth

title: Chunlei Ge
text:
Statistician & Data Scientist · PhD in Statistics, UBC Okanagan · Kelowna, BC
I am a statistician who builds models that stay reliable when data are messy, sparse or expensive to collect. I completed my PhD in Statistics at the University of British Columbia (Okanagan) in 2026, where my research combined differential equations with nonparametric regression to estimate growth and decay curves from limited data, with applications in fire science, epidemiology and oncology.
Alongside research, I spent several years as a graduate teaching assistant for mathematics, statistics and data courses, so I am used to explaining technical results to people who aren’t statisticians. I also hold an MA in Statistics from York University.
I’m looking for roles in statistics, data science and analytics where careful modelling makes a real difference to decisions.
